title: The Defense of Aelthor
dek: The Heavenly Host reaches Aelthor behind an eclipse and a radiant storm. The defenders hold through repeated waves, lost soldiers and a temporal incarnate, then face the cost of the victory and Aria’s call to take the war to heaven.

facts.People: Magnus; Adelia; Elenia; Scribonia; Olokun; Eugene; Aria; the Zarathian defenders
facts.Outcome: The defense holds; hundreds or perhaps thousands are killed

body:
The defenders gathered at Aelthor while an eclipse darkened behind the approaching clouds. The usual boasts and cheers had stopped. Ships brought soldiers downriver, a last vessel left the lighthouse, and the commanders tried to prepare a defense against an army they could barely see.

The assault would reach past the front lines into the spellcasters, sharpen the commanders’ disagreements, and leave hundreds or perhaps thousands dead. Olokun’s finishing blow would hold the city. What the survivors should do with that victory would remain fiercely disputed.

The last ship at the lighthouse

The company gathered in Zarathis before ships took them downriver toward the coast. The towns were quiet. Soldiers who usually answered danger with boasts now watched the coming assault in silence. Eugene thought of his father going to war and wondered whether he too had been afraid. Olokun could offer the frightened troops little more than a determined smile.

An eclipse darkened the sea beyond Aelthor’s walls. A last vessel was evacuating the lighthouse before the radiant cloud swallowed its spire. Waves struck the defenses while the sky turned red, then vanished behind the enemy’s cover. Aria’s ship remained visible for a little longer, flying its flag into the weather. Small as it looked against the storm, the sight steadied the watching people.

When Aria docked, the soldiers took their final positions. Adelia offered her healing potions and explained how staying nearby would improve them. Aria mistook the advice for an order; Adelia answered that it was only a suggestion. The other defenders prepared wards, potions and spells. Their need to fight together had not made them comfortable with one another.

What the commanders could agree on

Aria held the foremost line. Arandiel and Tarwen covered flanks, while battalions reported to the adventurers. Olokun took his place with the Emerald Veil’s mages and told them to support the soldiers and strike enemies closing on their position. Magnus placed himself where he could direct the archers. Scribonia and his simulacrum moved in step, their doubled footsteps briefly making Olokun laugh.

A Verdant Circle mage brought Eugene a choice. The Circle’s wise ones could drive away the concealing clouds or use them to call lightning onto the approaching enemy. Eugene chose lightning. The mage warned that the storm could strike friends too if they stood too close to its targets.

Elenia wanted a controlled defense. She urged the fighters to let the enemy come within reach of their own front line. The Silver Star should keep its distance and finish weakened targets; the Emerald Veil should conserve its biggest spells and support the formation. Her cavalry could then take the enemies funneled toward it. Magnus agreed that the commanders needed to work together.

The cause of the attack was already troubling them. Elenia suspected Aria had obtained the artifact they had sought. Scribonia agreed that she might have, but refused to treat innocent lives as an acceptable price. Olokun’s answer was immediate: whatever their suspicions, they were there to protect the realm.

The clouds open

The Heavenly Host kept its approach hidden until it burst through the cloud at the beach. Angels pressed toward the defenders. Magnus directed volleys from the archers. Scribonia protected the cavalry with spectral silk, while his simulacrum sent a great mothlike dragon into the fighting. Olokun moved between threatened positions, trying to keep the attackers away from the mages.

Elenia repeatedly called the front line back within the supporting formation. The defenders saw the fighting differently: she believed the plan was being ignored, while Scribonia and Magnus thought they were following it. When Eugene needed help, Magnus stayed forward to support him. Elenia came down from her vantage point as the enemy began picking at those behind the line.

An archangel destroyed Scribonia’s simulacrum. Eugene answered with contaminated power. His second blast brought the creature down, and its soul twisted into something claimed by Death. The nearby soldiers recoiled. Magnus, who had been criticized for such power himself, praised Eugene and urged others to use Delerium too.

Another angel drove through the troops with its mace. The first attackers were only a vanguard, and more were coming. Lightning from the Verdant Circle struck the enemy without hitting their allies that time. Aria charged onto the beach and cut down an archon. Elenia tried to banish the invaders rather than kill them, while the soldiers continued to fall.

The fight reaches the spellcasters

The next archangel moved with a different speed. Sundial symbols appeared around it as it bent time and flashed toward the rear. Eugene fell on its way through. Scribonia drew him closer and tried to intervene, but the angel’s control of time was stronger. Later he closed Eugene’s eyes and turned back to the battle, believing him dead.

Adelia raised her staff, Beacon of Hope, and drove enemies away with banishment. Olokun covered her movement and left stunned enemies for Aria to finish. Aria shouted that they were not to touch her Olokun, then complained when he moved the wrong way and spoiled the attack she had prepared. Their exchange happened amid a defense that was steadily losing soldiers.

A huge chromatic cloud came out of the storm. Within it was an incarnate: a vessel filled with a god’s might. It crossed the field with terrible speed and released temporal force through the mages at the back. It announced the wrath of Aionia and accused them of meddling with what was not theirs.

Elenia tried to ask what had provoked the attack. The vessel gave no useful answer. Aria declared that the gods did not care about mortals. Scribonia accused her of knowing the real cause; she suggested the relic search or Tiamat, without offering the company an agreed explanation. Olokun ordered them to stop arguing and protect the people still within reach. Around them, the army was bending under the assault.

Olokun’s final blow

Magnus struck with his own magic and moved to help Aria. Elenia felt a weakness open in an enemy’s defenses. The defenders kept fighting across the broken positions, but the incarnate’s next cosmic burst knocked Olokun down and staggered even Aria. Elenia brought him back up with healing. The force that had reached the back line was still loose among them.

Scribonia had become furious with Aria and the secrets between them. He attempted a spell against her, which failed around her defenses. Then he warned everyone to clear space: he intended to bring down a Meteor Swarm whether anyone remained in the way or not. Elenia called out that healing was coming and told the others to make room for it.

The meteors never fell. Olokun recovered, ran back toward the incarnate and struck it twice. His final blow unmade the creature into cosmic dust. He was relieved that Scribonia had not cast, and quietly apologized to Aionia after the giant vanished.

The day was won. The destruction did not vanish with the attacker. Hundreds, perhaps thousands, lay dead. No precise final casualty count was established. The defenders had held Aelthor, but the victory had cracked the people and forces that held it.

Aria above the rubble

Aria climbed to the highest point in the wreckage with blood on her blade and anger on her face. Her cloak was torn. She called attention to the sky and the enemies the defenders had brought down. The gods had sent their judgment, she told the survivors, and mortals had stood against it.

She demanded an answer in kind. They would fight back, rise as equals and make the gates of heaven answer to them. Magnus raised his weapon with her and shouted for Zarathis. A voice near the shattered gate took up her name. Others answered until the cry spread through the ranks.

That acclaim was a real part of her authority. It belonged beside the soldiers she had defended and the people who had watched her fight. It did not make every survivor share her answer to the battle. Olokun stood apart in grief for the mages. Elenia was already among the bodies. The city’s cultural champion had her crowd; the work of caring for the fallen was still going on below her.

The argument the battle leaves

Olokun asked Elenia to check on Eugene and offered a diamond if she needed one. Adelia also had magic ready. Elenia said she did not need the diamond, went to him and called him only unconscious. Eugene opened his eyes, drew breath, rolled onto his side and cried. Scribonia’s earlier belief that he had died and Elenia’s description did not settle the exact nature of his recovery.

Elenia kept searching the bodies for people she could still help and laying the dead in rows. Adelia used her own healing before leaving. The survivors would need to count the missing, mourn them and repair their defenses. The battle did not provide every casualty’s name or a complete military account of each part of the wall.

The next great argument was already present in Aria’s speech. Was survival a reason to strengthen the defenses, attempt negotiation, or take an army into the gods’ own war? At the council that followed, bereaved families and the losses at Aelthor would be invoked on every side. Their disagreement began with people they had failed to save, and with different ideas about how to keep it from happening again.
